notes.meaning: People brought word to David that the Philistines were attacking the town of Keilah. The raiders were stealing freshly harvested grain from the outdoor threshing floors. Even though Saul was the reigning king, the people turned to David for help because Saul was ignoring his duty to protect the land.

David did not rush into battle on his own impulse, but asked the Lord for guidance. He wanted to know if it was right to fight the enemy without orders from King Saul. God answered David clearly, telling him to attack the Philistines and rescue Keilah.

David's soldiers were terrified to march to Keilah. They were already living in fear of Saul while hiding in their home territory of Judah. They worried that fighting the Philistine army on the border would trap them between two deadly enemies.

David prayed to the Lord a second time to reassure his frightened men. God patiently confirmed His earlier command and gave a clear promise of victory. The Lord promised that He would personally hand the Philistines over to David.

David and his men marched to Keilah and won a crushing victory over the Philistines. They drove off the enemy's cattle to make up for the grain that had been stolen. In this way, David fully rescued the people of Keilah from danger.

When the priest Abiathar escaped the slaughter of his family and fled to David, he brought along the sacred priestly vest, called the ephod. This special garment held the holy stones used to ask God for answers. Having the high priest and the ephod gave David direct access to God's guidance while he was on the run.

When Saul heard that David was inside Keilah, he wrongly claimed that God had handed David over to him. He thought David had trapped himself by going into a walled city with gates and heavy bars. Saul foolishly believed God was helping his wicked scheme just because circumstances seemed favorable.

Saul gathered all his soldiers for war, pretending he was organizing a national campaign. His true goal was to trap and destroy David and his men inside Keilah. Saul abused his royal authority by using the nation's army for a personal grudge.

David discovered that Saul was secretly plotting his destruction. Instead of relying on his own wits, David asked Abiathar the priest to bring the holy ephod. He turned immediately to God to find out what to do next.

David prayed with deep respect, calling himself God's servant and addressing the Lord as the God of Israel. He shared the reports he had received that Saul was coming to destroy the entire town just to kill him. David cared more about the lives of the innocent citizens than his own safety.

David asked two urgent questions: whether the leaders of Keilah would hand him over, and whether Saul would truly march down. God answered the question about Saul first, telling David that Saul was indeed coming. The Lord answered what Saul intended to do if David chose to stay.

David then asked again if the people of the city would surrender him and his men to Saul. The Lord told him that they would hand him over. Even though David had just saved their lives, the frightened citizens would still betray him to save themselves from Saul's wrath.

David and his men, who now numbered about six hundred, left Keilah right away and kept moving wherever they could find shelter. When Saul heard that David had escaped, he called off his march. David chose to leave quietly so that the city would not be harmed.

David lived in natural rock fortresses in the rugged hill country of the Wilderness of Ziph. Saul searched for him every single day with relentless hatred. Yet Saul could never capture David because God refused to let David fall into his hands.

David hid in a wooded area called Horesh within the Wilderness of Ziph. He learned that Saul had set out with the deliberate goal of taking his life. This was a dark and dangerous time of constant threat for David.

Saul's son Jonathan slipped away to find David in the woods. Instead of bringing soldiers or money, Jonathan encouraged David by pointing his faith back to God's promises. A true friend helps us rely on the Lord when we are afraid.

Jonathan told David not to fear, promising that Saul would never capture him. He acknowledged that David was chosen to be king over Israel, and Jonathan humbly offered to serve as his second-in-command. Jonathan pointed out that even his father Saul knew deep down that God's plan could not be stopped.

David and Jonathan made a sacred promise of lifelong friendship before the Lord. After this meeting, David remained in the woods while Jonathan went back to his home. This was the very last time the two close friends ever saw each other on earth.

Men from the district of Ziph traveled to Saul's capital in Gibeah to betray David. They reported exactly where David was hiding among the hills and woods. Even though they belonged to David's own tribe of Judah, they chose to turn him over to his enemy.

The Ziphites invited the king to come down whenever he pleased. They promised that they would take full responsibility for handing David over to the royal troops. They volunteered this wicked service without Saul even having to ask.

Saul blessed the Ziphites in the name of the Lord, thanking them for showing him pity. He was so blinded by his own hatred that he used religious words to praise people who were betraying an innocent man. Saul felt sorry for himself and treated an act of betrayal as kindness.

Saul told the informants to go back and gather more details about David's habits and hideouts. He wanted to know who had seen David and exactly where his tracks led. Saul claimed that David was extremely clever and would easily slip away if they were not careful.

Saul ordered them to map out every single hiding place and bring back confirmed facts before he marched. Once he had certain proof, he vowed to hunt David through every family clan in Judah until he found him. Saul was convinced that careful planning would guarantee his success.

The Ziphites went home ahead of Saul to keep watch. In the meantime, David and his men had already moved further south into the Wilderness of Maon. They stayed in the dry wasteland valley, trying to stay ahead of the king's search parties.

Saul and his soldiers marched down to hunt David in Maon. When David was warned that Saul was coming, he moved down into a rocky stronghold. Saul received word of this new location and set out in hot pursuit.

Saul marched along one side of a mountain ridge while David and his men fled along the opposite side. David was rushing desperately to escape, but Saul's larger force was spreading out to surround and capture them. A single mountain stood like a wall between David and certain death.

Just as Saul's soldiers were closing the trap, an urgent messenger arrived with shocking news. The Philistines had launched a sudden invasion into the land. God used this unexpected raid to stop Saul in his tracks at the very last second.

Saul had to abandon his chase to fight off the Philistine invaders. Because Saul was pulled away right as he was about to seize David, the place was named Sela-hammahlekoth, which means the Rock of Separation. God proved that He can rescue His people even when escape seems impossible.

After Saul marched away, David left the area and found safety in the natural strongholds of En-gedi. This rocky region near the Dead Sea was full of cliffs and deep caves that provided excellent hiding spots. There David found a safe shelter to rest and worship God.
